summary: To support internationalization and a more diverse Internet community, the RFC Series needs to allow non-ASCII characters. English remains the required language, but future RFCs will be encoded in UTF-8. This informational document describes how non-ASCII characters are used in RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7997 explains how RFCs may use characters beyond ASCII. It describes where those characters are allowed and how authors can identify them so readers and search tools can interpret the documents.

questions: how are non-latin author names written in rfcs
subtitle: Rules for using characters beyond ASCII in RFCs while keeping documents readable and searchable.

tldr.problem: ASCII-only RFCs made it difficult to represent some names and internationalized protocol content clearly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC Series uses UTF-8 and permits non-ASCII characters under rules for readability, search, Unicode identification, XML markup, and ASCII alternatives.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7997 updates RFC 7322 and has itself been updated by RFC 9920.

facts.label: Unicode code point notation
facts.value: U+ followed by the hexadecimal value

today: RFC 7997 is Informational, updates RFC 7322, and has been updated by RFC 9920.

sections.title: From ASCII to UTF-8
sections.content:
The RFC Series used ASCII because English text could be displayed on a wide range of systems. The RFC explains that readable internationalized content calls for allowing a broader range of characters.

RFCs support UTF-8 as the default character encoding and allow Unicode characters. Non-ASCII characters should be limited to where they are needed. The RFC Editor may reject code points that do not render adequately in publication formats and rendering engines.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs can use characters beyond ASCII when needed. Authors should use them selectively so documents remain readable across systems.

sections.title: Search and Readability Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC gives two basic requirements. Searches of RFC indexes and databases should return expected results and support appropriate Unicode string matching. RFCs should also display correctly across a wide range of readers and browsers.

Readers whose systems lack a needed font must still be able to understand the publication formats and XML. If non-ASCII characters reduce readability, the RFC Editor may request alternate text. The Editor may ask reviewers to check the meaning and form of words written entirely in non-ASCII characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Readers need to be able to find RFC text in indexes and read it on different systems. If a character cannot be displayed clearly, the RFC needs another way to identify it.

sections.title: Person and Company Names
sections.content:
When an individual's name uses a script outside the Unicode Latin blocks, the RFC includes an author-provided ASCII-only identifier in parentheses immediately after the name. This rule applies in the header, acknowledgements, and references.

Company names use valid Unicode. If a company name includes characters outside the Latin and Latin Extended scripts, an author-provided ASCII-only identifier is required to help with searching and indexing.
sections.plainLanguage: Some names use writing systems that search tools may not handle consistently. The RFC pairs those names with an ASCII-only form to support reading and search.

sections.title: Identifying Characters in Text
sections.content:
When a non-ASCII character is needed to understand or use a protocol, the text must give its Unicode code point in U+ notation. Authors are encouraged to show the character itself and its Unicode name in capital letters as well. The RFC gives several acceptable combinations of these forms.

Code components generally use fixed-width fonts. Authors should not expect Unicode normalization forms to be preserved; if a particular form matters, the RFC should say so. Tables follow the same character-identification rules as regular text.
sections.plainLanguage: When a character matters to a protocol, identify it with its Unicode code point. Showing the character and its name can also help readers recognize it.

sections.title: References, XML, and Security
sections.content:
Reference entries must be in English and have ASCII text available for their subfields. Non-ASCII additions are allowed at the author's discretion, and the RFC Editor may request a review. Keywords and citation tags must use ASCII characters only.

When an ASCII alternative is required, authors must include it in an ascii attribute in the XML markup described by RFC 7991. The RFC says that valid Unicode matching the expected text must be verified to preserve expected behavior and protocol information.
sections.plainLanguage: Some document fields must remain searchable in ASCII, and required ASCII alternatives go in XML attributes. The text must also be checked to ensure the Unicode characters match what the RFC expects.
